periods.activity_title: Mapping Our School — A Green School Vision
periods.textbook_anchor: Green School — Walk around the school and create its map, including main building, playground, garden, water tanks, school gate and pathways (p. 56)
materials: plain A4 paper or notebook pages
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 56 — campus map activity illustration

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads aloud the opening conversation between Aasha and Mohit from Textbook p. 56, then poses the question: 'What would a school that saves water, manages waste and has plenty of green plants look like?' Students share brief ideas orally.

Students walk around the school campus in a quiet, orderly group (or look out of windows and recall familiar areas). They note key features — building blocks, playground, garden beds, water tanks, gate, and connecting paths.

Back at their seats, students draw a simple map of their school on plain paper, labelling each feature they observed. They use Textbook p. 56 as a prompt to check they have not missed any category of feature.

Students add a small legend to their map using colour: green for garden areas, blue for water points, yellow for buildings. They write one sentence below the map: 'One thing I noticed that could make our school greener is ___.'
Teacher invites two or three students to share what they noticed and recorded, closing the unit by affirming that careful observation is the first step toward improving any shared space.

periods.implied_lo: Students can record observations of a shared environment by creating a labelled map that identifies key features and one improvement opportunity.
periods.section_context: School campus walk, main building, playground, garden, water tanks, school gate, pathways, green school concept.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students: 'Which part of our school feels the most looked-after, and which part needs the most care?' — this open question surfaces varied observations and invites students to name the school's strengths alongside its gaps. Keep the walk unhurried enough for children to look and note, not just stroll.

periods.activity_title: School Explorer Teams — Structured Campus Inquiry
periods.textbook_anchor: Be a School Explorer! — Form explorer teams (Water Watchers, Electricity Savers, Waste Warriors, Green Guardians, Traffic Trackers) and observe the school environment using structured prompts (p. 57)
materials: printed or hand-written team role cards (one per group)

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the five School Explorer roles — Water Watchers, Electricity Savers, Waste Warriors, Green Guardians, and Traffic Trackers — and distributes students into groups. Each group receives a brief role card listing two or three specific things to look for on the campus.

Teams carry out their structured observation walk: Water Watchers check for dripping or running taps; Electricity Savers check for lights and fans left on in empty spaces; Waste Warriors look for litter and check whether bins are present and labelled; Green Guardians count or name plants and trees and check their condition; Traffic Trackers observe movement near the school gate and note any safety concerns. Each student records at least two findings in their notebook.

Back in class, each team takes two minutes to share their two most important findings with the class. The teacher notes key findings on the board under the five headings. After all teams have shared, students briefly discuss: 'Which finding surprised you most and why?'

Students write one sentence in their notebooks: 'Our team found that ___. We think this matters because ___.' Teacher closes by noting that observation without recording is easily forgotten — what they wrote today is the evidence base for future action.

periods.implied_lo: Students can carry out a structured group inquiry using assigned roles and observation prompts, and report findings with a brief justification.
periods.section_context: School Explorer Teams, Water Watchers, Electricity Savers, Waste Warriors, Green Guardians, Traffic Trackers, leaking taps, wasted electricity, litter, plants and trees, traffic at school gate.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Before the walk, ask students: 'What do you predict your team will find — a little of the problem, or a lot?' — revisiting the prediction after the walk sharpens scientific thinking. If time is short for the outdoor walk, allow groups to observe from corridors and windows rather than cancelling the activity.

periods.textbook_anchor: Waste Management — Make paper chits with item names or drawings, label three boxes (green/wet, blue/dry, recycler), sort chits and discuss correctness box by box (p. 61)
materials: small paper chits or sticky notes (30–40 per class set)
green, blue, and neutral labels for the boxes
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 61 — waste sorting activity illustration showing items

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly explains waste categories — wet waste (food peels, leftovers), dry waste (paper, plastic), and items for recyclers (old newspapers, glass) — and the colour coding: green bin for wet, blue bin for dry. Students open Textbook p. 61 to see the illustrated items and scan them quickly.

In groups of five or six, students write or draw item names on their paper chits — they may use the textbook illustration and add items from their own school or home experience. Each group prepares its three labelled boxes.

One student at a time picks a chit, reads it aloud, and places it in the box they think is correct. Other group members may quietly disagree; all decisions stand until the review phase. Groups work through all their chits.

Groups take one box at a time, read out its contents, and the class discusses whether each item was placed correctly. The teacher facilitates using Textbook p. 61 as the reference, noting any items that generated disagreement and asking students to explain their reasoning.

Students write one answer in notebooks from Textbook p. 59: the colour of the bin for dry waste and wet waste. Teacher draws together the unit by asking: 'What makes getting this right matter for the people who handle our waste after us?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can classify everyday materials into correct waste categories by applying the criteria of wet, dry, and recyclable, and justify their sorting decisions.
periods.section_context: Wet waste, dry waste, recycler items, green bin, blue bin, paper chits, food peels, leftovers, old newspapers, waste segregation.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt students to think about the people who handle waste after it leaves the bin — traditional recyclers known by different names in different regions have long practised community-based material recovery; ask students what recyclers in their own area collect and where those materials go. Group the class so that students with different home waste practices are in the same team.

periods.activity_title: Waste Consequences — Discussion and Role Reflection
periods.textbook_anchor: Waste Management — Discuss what happens if waste is not separated, and how students can make sanitation workers' work easier and safer (p. 62)

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the question from Textbook p. 62: 'What happens if we do not separate our waste?' Students think silently for one minute, then share with a partner. Three or four pairs share with the class; the teacher notes key consequences on the board (spread of disease, contamination of recyclables, extra burden on workers).

Teacher shifts to the second discussion prompt from Textbook p. 62: 'What can we do to make the work of sanitation workers easier and safer?' Students brainstorm in small groups of three, listing at least four actions. Groups share their ideas; the teacher compiles a class list on the board.

Students write their own response to both discussion questions in their notebooks — at least two sentences per question — drawing on the class list as a resource but using their own words and examples from their school or neighbourhood.

Teacher invites students to respond to this question: 'If a sanitation worker visited our class today, what one thing would you want to tell them and what one thing would you want to ask them?' Students share orally. Teacher closes by affirming that dignified, practical support for all workers in a community is a form of civic care.

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain the consequences of poor waste practices for community health and worker safety, and propose concrete actions to improve waste management.
periods.section_context: Unseparated waste consequences, disease spread, recyclable contamination, sanitation workers, dignity of labour, waste management improvement actions.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students: 'Has anyone in your family ever spoken to a sanitation worker or seen what they do? What did you notice?' — this grounds the discussion in real experience. Keep the tone one of genuine appreciation and problem-solving rather than blame.

periods.activity_title: Black and White Tiles — Heat Absorption Inquiry
periods.textbook_anchor: Let Us be Cool! — Paint two tiles or stones one black and one white, place under the Sun, touch and compare their temperatures (p. 62)
materials: two similar flat stones or tiles
a sunny window ledge or outdoor space
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 62 — illustration of the black and white tile activity

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks: 'Have you ever sat on a black surface in the sun and then a white surface? What did you notice?' Students share briefly. Teacher introduces the inquiry question from Textbook p. 62: which colour surface absorbs more heat?

In pairs, students wrap or paint one stone/tile black and one white (or apply pre-cut paper). Both tiles are placed on a sunny window ledge or taken to an outdoor sunny spot. Students predict which will feel hotter and write their prediction in their notebooks.

While waiting for the tiles to heat up, students discuss the content from Textbook p. 62–63: why do trees, ventilated windows, and white roofs keep spaces cool? How does this connect to the black and white tile experiment? The teacher connects to the traditional practice of coating floors with cow dung and mud in many villages — asking students whether they have seen or heard of this practice and why it might keep a home cool.

Students carefully touch each tile and compare temperatures. They write in notebooks: which felt hotter, whether their prediction was right, and one sentence explaining why. The class compares results and the teacher draws out the principle of heat absorption versus reflection.

Students respond to the write prompt from Textbook p. 63: 'If you had to paint the roof of your school or home white, what would happen?' — two to three sentences in notebooks. Teacher summarises: colour and material choices in buildings affect the comfort of everyone inside.

periods.implied_lo: Students can investigate how surface colour affects heat absorption by comparing outcomes of a controlled test and linking the finding to real-world building and design choices.
periods.section_context: Black tile, white tile, Sun heat absorption, roof colour, white roof cooling, ventilated windows, trees for shade.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students: 'Can you think of any building in your area that stays unusually cool or hot? What does its roof or wall colour look like?' — this bridges the experiment to local architecture. Ensure students touch tiles cautiously and never leave them unattended outside.

periods.activity_title: Measuring a Drip — Quantifying Water Wastage
periods.textbook_anchor: Dripping Water — Let water drip from a tap or a pin-hole bottle, collect in a glass, measure time to fill, and calculate how many glasses would fill in one day (p. 64)
materials: one used plastic bottle with a small pin-hole
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 64 — dripping tap activity illustration

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook p. 64 and asks: 'How much water do you think a dripping tap wastes in a whole day?' Students make estimates orally. Teacher sets up the pin-hole bottle demonstration at the front while students copy the observation table into their notebooks.

The bottle drips into a glass. Students watch and note the time it takes for the glass to fill. The teacher guides students to calculate: if one glass fills in that many minutes, how many glasses fill in one hour, and then in one day? Students carry out the arithmetic in their notebooks.

Teacher facilitates a discussion using the two prompts from Textbook p. 64: 'What easy things can we do in school to prevent water wastage?' and 'How can we collect and use rainwater at home or in school?' Students share ideas in pairs, then the class compiles a list on the board.

Students write three concrete water-saving actions for their school in their notebooks, explaining why each would make a measurable difference. Teacher connects to the Jal Shakti Abhiyan campaign as a civic example of school-based water conservation at scale.

Teacher closes by asking: 'What surprised you most about today's measurement — did the number feel large or small? What does that tell us about small, everyday habits?' Students share one-word or one-phrase responses.

periods.implied_lo: Students can measure and calculate the cumulative scale of water lost through a small leak, and propose specific conservation actions grounded in that evidence.
periods.section_context: Dripping tap, pin-hole bottle, water collection, time measurement, daily water loss calculation, rainwater collection, Jal Shakti Abhiyan.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students: 'In your home, have you ever seen a tap dripping and ignored it? What would you do differently now?' — connecting the number they just calculated to a personal habit sharpens the value dimension. If a real dripping tap is accessible on campus, use it in place of the bottle.

periods.activity_title: Tree Temperature Experiment — Greenery as a Natural Cooler
periods.textbook_anchor: Greenery Around Us — Measure water temperature under a tree and under the Sun using a thermometer; record before and after readings (p. 66)
materials: a thermometer (one, shared with teacher guidance)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 66 — temperature measurement activity illustration

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks students to recall from the heat-absorption work in the cooling section: 'We found that colour affects how much heat a surface absorbs — what about shade from trees? Will water under a tree stay cooler than water in the Sun?' Students predict in writing in their notebooks.

Teacher (with one student helper) measures and records the temperature of water in both glasses — using Textbook p. 66 as the guide — before placing one glass under a tree (or in a well-shaded cool corner if outdoors is not available) and one on a sunny window ledge. Students note both starting temperatures.

While waiting for a temperature difference to develop, students complete the written tasks from Textbook p. 65: naming trees on the school campus or nearby, and noting which birds and insects they have seen near trees. Teacher prompts them to think about what these trees provide — shade, food, habitat, cleaner air.

Teacher retrieves both glasses and measures the temperature of each. Students record the new readings and calculate the difference. The class discusses: 'What do these readings tell us about having trees on a school campus?' Teacher connects to the Ladakh ice stupa tradition as an example of community-designed water management using natural principles.

Students write one sentence: 'Trees help keep our school cool because ___.' Teacher closes by affirming that greenery is not just decoration — it is a working part of the school's environmental system.

periods.implied_lo: Students can design and carry out a temperature comparison experiment, record paired readings, and use the data to explain the cooling role of trees in a built environment.
periods.section_context: Two glasses of water, thermometer, temperature under tree vs. under Sun, campus trees, birds and insects near trees, natural cooling.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students: 'If you had to choose where to sit on a hot afternoon — under a tree or in an open space — why? Now use your data to explain that choice scientifically.' Encourage students to name actual trees on their campus; regional tree names are equally valid and worth celebrating.

periods.activity_title: Traffic Safety Signboard — Design and Civic Reflection
periods.textbook_anchor: Traffic Signs — Find out and write at least three traffic rules; observe and write what happens at the school gate (p. 67)
materials: plain paper or card (one sheet per student)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 67 — traffic signs and school gate illustration

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with Thomas's scenario from the chapter: a concern about road accidents near school. Students discuss briefly: 'What have you observed at our school gate during arrival or dismissal?' They then open Textbook p. 67 and write at least three traffic rules they know or can read from the page.

Teacher reads the write prompt from Textbook p. 67: 'Think and write about what you saw at the school gate.' Students write three to four sentences describing actual behaviours — vehicles, pedestrians, crowding, safe or unsafe actions — they have observed.

Students design a safety signboard for the school gate on their card or plain paper. The signboard may use words, drawings, symbols, or a combination. It must communicate one clear safety message to drivers, parents, or fellow students arriving at school.

Students share their signboards in a brief gallery walk (laid on desks). They leave a small tick or a written word on any signboard whose message they find clear and useful. Class discusses: 'Which messages were clearest and why?' Also addresses the discussion prompt from Textbook p. 68: what else, beyond signboards, can students do to improve traffic near school?
Teacher closes by affirming that designing for public safety is a form of civic responsibility — students who identify a hazard and propose a solution are acting as active members of their community.

periods.implied_lo: Students can communicate a civic safety message through a designed visual artefact that applies knowledge of traffic rules and observed behaviour at a public place.
periods.section_context: Traffic rules, school gate observation, safety signboard design, words and symbols, civic responsibility, pedestrian and vehicle safety.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students: 'Who is your signboard really speaking to — drivers, students, parents, or all three? How does knowing your audience change the words or pictures you choose?' Encourage multilingual signs or regional scripts if students choose — this is a real public communication task.

periods.activity_title: Fire Drill Practice — Preparedness and Calm Response
periods.textbook_anchor: Fire Safety — Write where the fire extinguisher is kept, where the assembly point is, and what to do if there is a fire or smoke (p. 68–69)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 68–69 — fire drill steps illustration

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook p. 68 and asks two quick questions from the page: 'Where is the fire extinguisher in our school?' and 'Where is our assembly point?' Students who know answer; the teacher confirms or supplies the correct locations. Students write both answers in their notebooks.

Teacher reads through the six fire drill steps from Textbook p. 68–69 with the class — moving calmly to exits, crawling under smoke, avoiding hiding places, helping others safely, reaching the assembly point, and alerting staff. Students listen, then close their books and try to recall all six steps with a partner.

The class practises a classroom-level fire drill: teacher signals 'fire', students calmly leave their seats, move to the designated corridor or assembly route in a line, and arrive at the notional assembly point (or the classroom door if a full drill is not possible). Teacher observes and notes which steps students perform correctly and which need reinforcement.

Back in their seats, students write their answer to the prompt from Textbook p. 69: 'What should you do if there is a fire or if you smell smoke?' — in their own words, covering at least four of the six steps. Teacher reviews responses by asking three students to share.

Teacher closes by asking: 'Which step do you think is hardest to remember in a real emergency, and what can you do to make sure you remember it?' Students share briefly, cementing the habit of preparedness over panic.

periods.implied_lo: Students can recall and practise the correct sequence of actions for a fire emergency, and explain why calm, orderly behaviour matters more than speed.
periods.section_context: Fire extinguisher location, assembly point, six fire drill steps, smoke response, calm evacuation, fire safety preparedness.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students: 'Have you ever heard of a fire drill happening in a real building — a hospital, a hotel, or a cinema? Why do you think those places practise too?' — connecting the school drill to a wider civic safety culture. Coordinate with the school administration in advance if a full campus drill is intended.

periods.activity_title: Behaviour Scenarios — Group Discussion and Social Norms
periods.textbook_anchor: What We do Matters! — In small groups, discuss five scenarios of poor behaviour (queue-jumping, vandalism, littering, teasing, noise); share what you would do and how to prevent such incidents (p. 70)

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the section: 'The way we behave with others shapes whether a space feels welcoming or uncomfortable.' Students open Textbook p. 70 and read the five situations silently.

Students form five groups, one per situation from Textbook p. 70. Each group discusses: (1) what they would do if they saw the situation unfold, and (2) what steps could prevent it. One student in each group keeps brief notes of the group's ideas.

One representative from each group shares their group's conclusions with the class — what they would do and one prevention step. After each sharing, the class may add one brief observation. Teacher notes key ideas on the board under two columns: 'What I would do' and 'How to prevent it.'

Students write in their notebooks: 'The situation that I found most difficult to respond to was ___ because ___. One thing I can practise this week is ___.' Teacher closes by affirming that respect, kindness, and polite behaviour are demonstrated through everyday actions, not just intentions.

periods.implied_lo: Students can evaluate real-life scenarios of poor social behaviour, articulate a considered response, and propose prevention strategies grounded in community norms.
periods.section_context: Queue-jumping at water tap, vandalism of classroom bench, littering and copycat behaviour, teasing, noise in public park, civic behaviour, prevention strategies.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students: 'Why do you think the bystander in situation two says nothing — what makes it hard to speak up?' — exploring the psychology of bystander behaviour deepens the discussion beyond simple right and wrong. Ensure all five situations are covered even if some groups need brief prompting.

periods.activity_title: Happiness Tree — Collective Creation and School Pride
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Draw a large happiness tree on chart paper; each student adds a leaf with one action that makes school a happier place (p. 71)
materials: one large sheet of chart paper or a section of board paper
small cut leaf shapes in green paper (one per student) or students draw their own

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the closing reflection section of the chapter. One student or the teacher draws a large tree outline (trunk and bare branches) on chart paper. Teacher explains: each student will write one small action on a leaf — something any student could actually do that would make school a happier place.

Students think individually, then write their action on their leaf shape or on a drawn leaf. Teacher encourages variety — actions might relate to greetings, saving electricity, sharing space, including a lonely classmate, turning off taps, watering plants — drawing from all the themes of the chapter.

Students come up one by one to attach their leaf to the tree. Each reads their action aloud in one sentence. Teacher notes patterns: which themes come up most often? The completed tree is displayed on the board.

Students write a short letter in their notebooks using the prompt from Textbook p. 71: 'My School — My Happy Place', addressed to their teacher. The letter should include at least two things they genuinely appreciate about school and one thing they personally commit to doing differently.

Teacher reads two or three short excerpts from the letters (with student permission) and closes by reflecting that the happiness tree belongs to the whole class — every leaf on it is a promise made by someone in this room.

periods.implied_lo: Students can express appreciation for their school community through a creative collective artefact and a personal written commitment to a specific positive action.
periods.section_context: Happiness tree, leaves with student actions, greetings, electricity saving, sharing space, including others, personal commitment letter to teacher.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students: 'Which leaf on the tree do you think would make the biggest difference to the most people — and why?' — this encourages them to think about impact, not just intention. Preserve the tree display for a few days if possible; it reinforces community identity.

periods.activity_title: Perspective Diary — Writing from Another's Point of View
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Write a diary entry from the perspective of a wheelchair-using student, a student with a different mother tongue, or a sanitation worker at school (p. 71)

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the diary task from Textbook p. 71: students choose one of three perspectives — a student who uses a wheelchair, a student whose mother tongue is different from the medium of instruction, or a sanitation worker at school. Teacher asks: 'Before you begin writing, think: what would be easy in a school day for this person, and what might be difficult?'

Students write their diary entry — at least one full page — in their notebooks. The entry should include: what the person felt during the school day, what was easy or hard, and what made them smile or worry. Teacher circulates, offering prompts to students who are stuck: 'Where does this person spend most of their time in school? What would they notice that you might not?'

Three or four volunteers read their diary entries aloud. After each reading, the class briefly discusses: 'What did this perspective reveal that we might not have thought about?' Teacher notes any themes of inclusion, access, dignity, or comfort that emerge across the entries.

Teacher closes by connecting the diary task to the chapter's broader theme: 'A school is a happy place only if it feels that way for everyone in it — including people whose experience is different from our own.' Students reflect silently for one minute on one thing they will do differently.

periods.implied_lo: Students can write a sustained first-person account from a perspective other than their own, identifying specific experiences of ease or difficulty in a shared environment.
periods.section_context: Diary entry, wheelchair-using student perspective, different-mother-tongue student perspective, sanitation worker perspective, inclusion, access, dignity.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students: 'Is there anyone in our school — or in schools you know — whose experience might be like the person you are writing about? What have you noticed about how easy or hard things are for them?' Keep discussion grounded in empathy rather than pity. Accept all three perspective choices equally; no choice signals more sensitivity than another.

periods.activity_title: Dream School Speech and Peer Survey — Action and Voice
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Conduct a quick survey of five students and one teacher asking three questions about happiness, improvement, and kindness in school; record and present findings (p. 72)

time_bands.activity: Students carry out the survey from Textbook p. 72: they move around the classroom (or corridor) to ask five classmates and, if possible, one teacher the three questions — what makes them feel happy in school, what could be improved, and what kind thing they saw today. Students record responses in their notebooks.

Students return to their seats and write a brief summary of their survey findings: the most common 'happy' response, the most common improvement suggestion, and one kind act that was mentioned. They note what surprised them or what they learned from others.

Students write a one-minute speech for morning assembly on 'My Dream School', using the prompt from Textbook p. 72. The speech should mention what makes the school special, who helps it stay that way, and what every student can do. Students have eight minutes to draft and one minute to read silently to themselves.

Three or four students read their speeches aloud. The class applauds each. Teacher closes by connecting the speech and survey to the chapter's arc: every theme covered — greenery, water, waste, heat, traffic, fire safety, and social behaviour — is something every student can act on. The chapter's aspiration — a school that is green, safe, and happy — belongs to all of them.

periods.implied_lo: Students can gather, summarise, and present peer perspectives through a structured survey, and articulate a personal vision for improving a shared environment in spoken form.
periods.section_context: Peer survey, five students and one teacher, happiness in school, improvement suggestions, kind acts observed, dream school speech, morning assembly.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students before the survey: 'Do you think the teacher's answer and a student's answer will be the same or different? Why?' — setting up the comparison makes the data collection genuinely curious. Ensure the speech-writing prompt invites ambition — 'dream school' should feel expansive, not constrained to what currently exists.

coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Traffic Signs — Find out and write at least three traffic rules; observe and write what happens at the school gate (p. 67)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students write three traffic rules, note school gate observations, design a safety signboard for the gate, and evaluate peer signboards in a gallery walk.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can recall and practise the correct sequence of actions for a fire emergency, and explain why calm, orderly behaviour matters more than speed.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Fire extinguisher location, assembly point, six fire drill steps, smoke response, calm evacuation, fire safety preparedness.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Fire Safety — Write where the fire extinguisher is kept, where the assembly point is, and what to do if there is a fire or smoke (p. 68–69)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students locate fire safety features, review the six drill steps, practise a classroom evacuation, and write the correct response to a fire or smoke situation in their own words.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can evaluate real-life scenarios of poor social behaviour, articulate a considered response, and propose prevention strategies grounded in community norms.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Queue-jumping at water tap, vandalism of classroom bench, littering and copycat behaviour, teasing, noise in public park, civic behaviour, prevention strategies.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: What We do Matters! — In small groups, discuss five scenarios of poor behaviour (queue-jumping, vandalism, littering, teasing, noise); share what you would do and how to prevent such incidents (p. 70)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Five groups each discuss one real-life scenario of poor behaviour, share their response and prevention ideas with the class, and write a personal reflection on the hardest situation.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can express appreciation for their school community through a creative collective artefact and a personal written commitment to a specific positive action.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Happiness tree, leaves with student actions, greetings, electricity saving, sharing space, including others, personal commitment letter to teacher.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Draw a large happiness tree on chart paper; each student adds a leaf with one action that makes school a happier place (p. 71)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students co-create a happiness tree by contributing action-leaves, then write a personal letter to their teacher about what they love about school and one commitment they make.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can write a sustained first-person account from a perspective other than their own, identifying specific experiences of ease or difficulty in a shared environment.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Diary entry, wheelchair-using student perspective, different-mother-tongue student perspective, sanitation worker perspective, inclusion, access, dignity.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Write a diary entry from the perspective of a wheelchair-using student, a student with a different mother tongue, or a sanitation worker at school (p. 71)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students choose one of three perspectives and write a full diary entry describing a school day from that viewpoint, then share selected entries and discuss what each revealed.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can gather, summarise, and present peer perspectives through a structured survey, and articulate a personal vision for improving a shared environment in spoken form.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Peer survey, five students and one teacher, happiness in school, improvement suggestions, kind acts observed, dream school speech, morning assembly.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Conduct a quick survey of five students and one teacher asking three questions about happiness, improvement, and kindness in school; record and present findings (p. 72)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students conduct a five-student-plus-teacher survey, summarise their findings, draft a one-minute morning assembly speech on their dream school, and three or four students deliver their speeches.

assessment_items.question_text: Riya walks around her school and notices that the garden area has many plants, the water tanks are near the back building, and the gate opens onto a busy road. She draws a map and marks each feature with a different colour. What is the most important reason for including all these features on the map?

options.label: A
options.text: To copy what the textbook shows exactly.

options.label: B
options.text: To make the map look colourful and neat.

options.label: C
options.text: To record an accurate picture of the school environment that can be used to identify what needs improvement.

options.label: D
options.text: To show the teacher that the student walked the full route.

assessment_items.annotation: A correct map is not merely decorative — it is a tool for observation and improvement planning. Option B reflects the purpose of structured observation as articulated in the section.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can record observations of a shared environment by creating a labelled map that identifies key features and one improvement opportunity.

competency.competency_text: Explains the functioning of local institutions (family, school, bank/post office, market, and panchayat) in different forms (story, drawing, tabulating data, reports), and analyses their roles

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student focuses on aesthetics rather than function — they have not connected the map-making task to observation and analysis of the school environment.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student thinks the task is about compliance or showing effort rather than about gathering useful environmental data.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student treats the textbook as a template to replicate rather than as a prompt for original observation of their own school.

assessment_items.question_text: A School Explorer Team is checking the school for wasted electricity. They find three fans running in an empty staffroom and two lights on in the library where no one is reading. Write two things the team should record in their notebook and one recommendation they should make to the class.
expected_elements: Identification of at least two specific observations to record (e.g., fans running in empty staffroom; lights on in empty library).
A recommendation that addresses preventing the wastage — such as turning off appliances when rooms are empty, or placing reminders near switches.
The response should be framed as a team finding and a suggestion for action, not just a personal opinion.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any two clearly described observations that name the specific appliance and location. The recommendation must be actionable — 'save electricity' alone is insufficient without a specific step.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can carry out a structured group inquiry using assigned roles and observation prompts, and report findings with a brief justification.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: Two specific observations named with appliance type and location (fans in staffroom; lights in library).
A concrete recommendation such as switching off appliances when rooms are empty, or posting reminder signs at room exits.
Language that reflects a team role — 'our team found' or 'we recommend' — rather than a personal anecdote.

assessment_items.question_text: Arun's family has collected banana peels, used tea leaves, leftover rice, old newspapers, glass bottles, and worn-out plastic bags. Which of these should go into the BLUE bin?

options.label: A
options.text: All of the items listed above.

options.label: C
options.text: Old newspapers, glass bottles, and worn-out plastic bags.

options.label: D
options.text: Used tea leaves and banana peels.

assessment_items.annotation: Blue bin = dry waste (newspapers, glass, plastic). Green bin = wet waste (food peels, tea leaves, rice). Option B correctly identifies all three dry-waste items.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can classify everyday materials into correct waste categories by applying the criteria of wet, dry, and recyclable, and justify their sorting decisions.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has reversed the categories — placing wet waste in the blue bin indicates confusion between colour coding for wet and dry waste.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student selects only wet/food items and does not apply the dry-waste criterion — they may not have understood that blue means dry.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has not grasped that segregation means separating items, not grouping all waste together.

assessment_items.question_text: Priya's school does not separate wet and dry waste — everything goes into one big bin together. The sanitation workers who collect the waste find their work very difficult. Explain two problems caused by mixed waste, and describe two things Priya's school could do to make the sanitation workers' work easier and safer.
look_for: Two clearly articulated problems resulting from unseparated waste — such as spread of disease or bad smells from rotting food mixed with dry items; recyclable materials being spoiled or contaminated by wet waste; sanitation workers having to manually sort through mixed waste, increasing risk of injury or infection.

Two practical, school-level actions — such as placing labelled green and blue bins in every classroom and the canteen; teaching students the colour coding; ensuring bins are clearly marked and accessible.
A response that connects the problem to the effect on workers — not just on the environment in general — showing awareness of dignity and safety.
Specific and concrete language rather than vague generalisations ('we should be clean').
assessment_items.annotation: Strong responses name specific types of harm (contamination of recyclables; health risk from rotting matter) and specific actions (installing labelled bins; student awareness campaigns). Vague responses ('it creates problems' or 'we must be responsible') score lower.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain the consequences of poor waste practices for community health and worker safety, and propose concrete actions to improve waste management.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

look_for: Two specific consequences of mixed waste named with cause-and-effect reasoning (e.g., wet food waste spoils paper and glass, making recycling impossible; workers must touch mixed waste without being able to anticipate hazards).
Two concrete school actions with enough detail to be actionable (e.g., place colour-coded bins in each room with picture labels for younger students).
Awareness that the waste system includes multiple workers and stages — not just the act of throwing something away.
Respectful framing of sanitation workers' role — the response should not treat them as invisible or blame them.

assessment_items.question_text: Neha painted one stone black and one stone white and left both in the Sun for the same amount of time. When she touched them, the black stone felt much hotter than the white one. Which statement best explains this difference?

options.label: A
options.text: Black paint is thicker and traps heat inside the stone.

options.label: B
options.text: Dark colours absorb more of the Sun's heat, while light colours reflect it.

options.label: C
options.text: The black stone is heavier, so it stores more heat.

options.label: D
options.text: The white stone was kept in a shadier spot by mistake.

assessment_items.annotation: Option B correctly identifies the principle of heat absorption by colour — the scientific finding the activity is designed to build. The other options offer alternative (incorrect) causal explanations.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can investigate how surface colour affects heat absorption by comparing outcomes of a controlled test and linking the finding to real-world building and design choices.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student is confusing mass/weight with heat capacity — they have not connected colour to absorption behaviour.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student is doubting the fairness of the experiment rather than reading the result — this suggests they have not understood controlled testing.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student is constructing an intuitive but incorrect explanation about paint thickness — they lack the absorption-vs-reflection concept.

assessment_items.question_text: Karan times a dripping bottle and finds that it fills one glass of water in 20 minutes. He wants to know how many glasses of water would be wasted in one full day (24 hours). Show your working and write the answer. Then write one specific action his school could take to reduce this kind of water loss.
expected_elements: Correct calculation: 60 ÷ 20 = 3 glasses per hour; 3 × 24 = 72 glasses per day — or equivalent correct arithmetic shown step by step.
One specific, school-level conservation action — such as reporting leaking taps to the school office, using a drip-catcher, or assigning a Water Watcher role to check taps daily.
The action should be framed as something a student or school can actually do, not a general statement about saving water.
assessment_items.annotation: The calculation should show at least two steps. Award full marks for the correct final answer (72 glasses) with working shown and a concrete conservation action. Partial marks if working is shown but arithmetic error occurs, or if the action is vague.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can measure and calculate the cumulative scale of water lost through a small leak, and propose specific conservation actions grounded in that evidence.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

expected_elements: Step 1: 60 ÷ 20 = 3 glasses per hour (or equivalent reasoning).
Step 2: 3 × 24 = 72 glasses per day.
One concrete conservation action with enough specificity to be actionable in a real school (not just 'close taps').

assessment_items.question_text: Class 5B placed one glass of water under a tree and another glass in direct sunlight. After an hour, the glass in the Sun was much warmer. Write two things this experiment tells us about the importance of trees in a school, and name one way the school could use this knowledge to make students more comfortable.
expected_elements: Two specific conclusions drawn from the experiment — such as: trees provide shade that keeps surrounding air and surfaces cooler; trees reduce the temperature difference between shaded and unshaded areas.
One practical application of the finding — such as planting trees near classrooms to reduce heat, placing benches under existing trees, or choosing shaded spots for outdoor activities.
Responses should be grounded in the temperature comparison, not just general claims about trees being 'good'.
assessment_items.annotation: Strong responses connect the temperature data to a specific campus application. Weak responses say trees are good without explaining why the experiment supports that. Regional tree names are equally acceptable.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can design and carry out a temperature comparison experiment, record paired readings, and use the data to explain the cooling role of trees in a built environment.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

expected_elements: Two conclusions explicitly linked to the experiment — temperature under tree vs. under Sun — not just general tree benefits.
One school-level application that uses the cooling principle (e.g., siting a reading corner or benches under trees; planning new tree planting near classrooms).
Evidence of understanding that trees are a functional part of the school environment, not just decoration.

assessment_items.task: Design a safety signboard for your school gate. Your signboard should communicate one clear message to drivers, parents, or students to make the area near the gate safer. Use words, pictures, or symbols — or a combination of all three.
assessment_items.scaffold: Think about: Who is your signboard speaking to — drivers, parents, or students arriving at school? What is the one most important safety message for that person? What words or pictures would make the message clear even to someone in a hurry? Write the traffic rule your signboard is based on. Then draw and label your signboard below.
format_of_output: A drawn and labelled signboard on the paper provided.
A written sentence naming the traffic rule the signboard is based on.
A written sentence identifying who the signboard is aimed at.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any safety message that is grounded in a real traffic rule and communicated clearly through visual design. Regional language text on the signboard is equally valid and should be credited. Signboards that identify a specific audience and use appropriate visual language (symbols, bold text, clear imagery) show stronger understanding.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can communicate a civic safety message through a designed visual artefact that applies knowledge of traffic rules and observed behaviour at a public place.

competency.competency_text: Explains the functioning of local institutions (family, school, bank/post office, market, and panchayat) in different forms (story, drawing, tabulating data, reports), and analyses their roles

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can translate a civic rule into a public communication artefact, showing understanding of audience, safety, and visual design.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold guides students to identify audience, select one focused message, and name the rule behind it — look for all three elements in the final output.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: signboard is visually clear, aimed at a specific audience, message is grounded in a named traffic rule, and design choices (bold text, symbols, colour) suit the context. Weak: signboard has a vague message ('be safe') with no rule cited and no clear audience identified.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find drawing difficult may produce a text-heavy signboard or use symbols only — both are valid. Students who wish to write in their home language or use local script should be encouraged; this reflects real-world multilingual signage.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Drawn and labelled signboard plus two written sentences.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Creating a public communication artefact is the mode used in the section; the written sentences ensure the reasoning behind the design is visible and assessable.

assessment_items.task: Your teacher calls 'Fire!' in the classroom. Show exactly what you would do — step by step — from the moment you hear the alarm to the moment you reach the assembly point. Act it out, and then write the steps in the correct order.
assessment_items.scaffold: As you act out or write: What is the very first thing you do when you hear 'Fire'? Do you run or walk — and why? What do you do if there is smoke near the floor? Should you hide under your desk or move toward the exit? How do you help a classmate who is scared? Where do you go after you leave the building?
format_of_output: A physical enactment of the six steps (observed by the teacher).
A written list of the six steps in correct order.
assessment_items.annotation: Assess both the physical enactment and the written list. The written list should match the six-step sequence from the chapter. A student who enacts correctly but writes out of order, or vice versa, should be given an opportunity to reconcile the two — the goal is internalised, transferable preparedness.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can recall and practise the correct sequence of actions for a fire emergency, and explain why calm, orderly behaviour matters more than speed.

competency.competency_text: Discusses how to prepare for emergency situations (smoke, fire, small injuries, burns, electrical safety, unseasonal rains, fallen trees) based on discussions with family and community, or personal experiences

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student has internalised an emergency preparedness sequence and can translate it into both physical behaviour and ordered written recall.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold prompts the key decision points within the drill — running vs. walking, smoke response, avoiding hiding, helping others, reaching the assembly point. Look for evidence that students answered each decision correctly.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: enactment is calm and sequential; written list covers all six steps in correct order with brief justification for at least one step (e.g., 'I walk, not run, so nobody gets knocked over'). Weak: student panics in enactment or writes steps out of order without reasoning.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students with mobility differences may describe or draw each step rather than enact physically — the cognitive and safety understanding is the same. Students may also write in their home language.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Performance enactment plus written step list.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Fire safety preparedness is a physical behaviour, not a written product — the performance task format matches the real outcome the section is developing.
OPEN_TASK.observation_rubric: Step 1 — Student responds calmly (does not shout or push). Step 2 — Student moves toward the exit without running. Step 3 — Student demonstrates crawling or low posture if smoke is mentioned. Step 4 — Student avoids 'hiding' gestures (under desk, in corner). Step 5 — Student demonstrates checking on or guiding a peer. Step 6 — Student arrives at a designated assembly point and waits calmly.

assessment_items.question_text: Read this situation: 'Rohan sees two students pushing each other to be first at the water tap while several others wait quietly. He wants to say something but is not sure what to do.' Explain what Rohan should do and why. Then describe one thing the class could put in place so this situation does not keep happening.
look_for: A clearly reasoned response about what Rohan should do — calmly reminding the students to queue, alerting a teacher, or modelling the correct behaviour himself — with a reason that connects to fairness or community norms.
Recognition that doing nothing (being a silent bystander) is also a choice with consequences — stronger responses name this tension.
One prevention measure that is concrete and classroom-level — such as a queue monitor role, a visible queue marker at the tap, or a class agreement about taking turns.
Language that reflects social norms from the chapter — respect, fairness, shared spaces — rather than just personal preference.
assessment_items.annotation: Strong responses address both the immediate action and the systemic prevention. Weak responses say only 'Rohan should tell the teacher' without reasoning or prevention. Accept any prevention measure that is realistic and student-initiated.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can evaluate real-life scenarios of poor social behaviour, articulate a considered response, and propose prevention strategies grounded in community norms.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

look_for: A specific, reasoned action for Rohan — not just 'he should do something' — with a justification grounded in fairness or queue norms.
Acknowledgment of the bystander dimension — it is harder to speak up than to stay quiet, and the response should show the student understands that.
A prevention measure that is structural or procedural (a system, role, or rule) rather than just relying on individuals to be better.
Consistent use of community-norm language — shared space, fairness, respect — drawn from the chapter's discussion framework.

assessment_items.task: Add your leaf to the class Happiness Tree. On your leaf, write one action — something you can actually do in school — that would make school a happier place for more people. Then write a short letter (four to six sentences) to your teacher titled 'My School — My Happy Place'. In your letter, share two things you genuinely appreciate about your school and one specific thing you commit to doing differently.
assessment_items.scaffold: For your leaf: Choose an action that helps more than just yourself — something that makes the school better for classmates, younger students, or staff. For your letter: Think about a moment in school that felt warm or welcoming. What made it feel that way? Who helped create that feeling? What is one habit you want to build that connects to what you have explored in this chapter?
format_of_output: A written action on a leaf shape (one sentence).
A four-to-six-sentence personal letter to the teacher.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any action that is genuinely school-focused, realistic, and aimed at benefiting others. The letter should name specific appreciations (not just 'I like school') and a specific commitment (not just 'I will be good'). Both outputs together show the student's capacity to move from general appreciation to personal action.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can express appreciation for their school community through a creative collective artefact and a personal written commitment to a specific positive action.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can translate chapter learning into a personal community-oriented commitment and articulate genuine appreciation for a shared institution.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold directs students to choose actions that benefit others and to ground their letter in a real, felt moment. Look for specificity in both the leaf action and the letter's appreciations.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: leaf action names a specific, other-directed behaviour (e.g., 'greet the canteen worker every day'); letter names two concrete appreciations and one specific new habit with a reason. Weak: vague leaf ('be kind'); letter repeats 'I like my school' without specific detail or a real commitment.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students may write in their home language, draw their commitment as a picture with a caption, or dictate to a peer-scribe — the depth of thinking is the assessment target, not the mode of recording.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Leaf action plus short personal letter.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The happiness tree is the chapter's collective creative artefact; the personal letter ensures the creative act is grounded in individual reflection and specific commitment.

assessment_items.task: Choose one of the following: (a) A student who uses a wheelchair, (b) A student whose mother tongue is different from the language used in class, or (c) A sanitation worker at your school. Write a diary entry of at least one full page from that person's point of view, describing a day at school. Include: what they felt, what was easy or hard, and what made them smile or worry.
assessment_items.scaffold: Before you write, think: Where does this person spend most of their day in school? What parts of the school building or routine might be easy for them, and what parts might be difficult? What small moments — a kind word, a confusing sign, a blocked ramp, a heavy bin — might stand out to them? What would they hope others in school understood about their experience?
format_of_output: A sustained first-person diary entry of at least one full page.
The diary entry must include at least one moment of ease and one moment of difficulty, and one emotion named explicitly.
assessment_items.annotation: All three perspective choices are equally valid — do not penalise a student for choosing the sanitation worker over the wheelchair user, or vice versa. Strong entries show specific, concrete observations (a blocked ramp, a word they did not understand, a heavy load) rather than generalised sympathy. The student need not have personal experience of the perspective to write a strong response — imagination guided by the scaffold is sufficient.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can write a sustained first-person account from a perspective other than their own, identifying specific experiences of ease or difficulty in a shared environment.

competency.competency_text: Explains the functioning of local institutions (family, school, bank/post office, market, and panchayat) in different forms (story, drawing, tabulating data, reports), and analyses their roles

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can inhabit and articulate a perspective different from their own, using the school as a context to analyse how the same institution functions differently for different people.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold prompts students to identify specific physical and social features of the school day from the chosen perspective. Look for evidence that students engaged with the scaffold's questions — not just wrote general feelings.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: entry names specific school features (a ramp, a sign, a bin route, a lesson in an unfamiliar language), gives concrete moments of ease and difficulty, and names at least one emotion with a reason. Weak: entry says 'they felt sad because school was hard' without any specific observation or detail.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students may write in a mix of languages if the person they are writing as would plausibly do so (e.g., a student with a different mother tongue might mix languages in their diary). Accept drawings with captions as a supplement to or replacement for prose if a student has difficulty with extended writing.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The diary form requires sustained perspective-taking and personal voice — it is the mode specified in the section and the one that best reveals depth of empathy and analytical thinking about inclusion.

assessment_items.question_text: Meena surveys five classmates and her teacher using three questions: (1) What makes you feel happy in school? (2) What could be improved? (3) What kind thing did you see today? She finds that four out of six people mentioned friends and kindness as what makes them happy, and three people said the toilets need to be cleaner. Write two things Meena learned from comparing the student and teacher answers, and describe how she could present her findings clearly to the class.
expected_elements: Two specific observations Meena could make by comparing student and teacher responses — such as: both groups value kindness; teachers and students may agree or disagree on what needs improving; the teacher's 'kind thing' observation may differ from students' because they see the school from a different vantage point.
A clear method for presenting findings to the class — such as reading out a summary, drawing a simple tally on the board, or sharing the most common response from each question.
The response should show understanding that a survey produces comparative data, not just individual opinions.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any two valid comparative observations. The presentation method should be realistic within a classroom. Regional context may shape what students identify as 'kind acts' — this is valid and should be credited.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can gather, summarise, and present peer perspectives through a structured survey, and articulate a personal vision for improving a shared environment in spoken form.

competency.competency_text: Explains the functioning of local institutions (family, school, bank/post office, market, and panchayat) in different forms (story, drawing, tabulating data, reports), and analyses their roles

expected_elements: Two comparative observations drawn from the survey data — at least one that explicitly compares student and teacher responses (agreement, disagreement, or different focus areas).
A specific, feasible presentation method for sharing findings with the class (spoken summary, tally on board, reading out the most common answer for each question).
Evidence that the student understands survey data as a tool for understanding a community, not just collecting random opinions.
